summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity, the shifted pairs \((a_{3773+k}+1,a_{3774+k}+1)\) evolve by the Fibonacci matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\); a modular exponentiation modulo \(195318521017\) at \(k=249580073233\) shows that both corresponding consecutive terms are divisible by this modulus. Their gcd is therefore at least \(2\), but for positive \(x,y\) with \(g=\gcd(x,y)>1\), the recurrence value \(g+(x+y)/g\) cannot equal \(1+x+y\), contradicting the asserted identity at the next index.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n},\quad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2})\quad(n\geq3).
\]
The division is exact because \(g_n\) divides both summands in the numerator.

We will show that the first of the three asserted formulas cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Since the conjecture asserts all three formulas simultaneously, this is enough to disprove the whole conjecture. The second formula and the Fibonacci closed form will not be needed.

First note that every \(a_n\) is positive. This is immediate for \(a_1,a_2\). Inductively, if the preceding terms are positive, their gcd is positive, and hence the recurrence expresses the next term as a sum whose first summand is positive.

Assume, for contradiction, that the conjecture is true. In particular, assume that
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}                                      \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\geq3775\). Equivalently, for every integer \(k\geq0\),
\[
a_{3775+k}=1+a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k}.                         \tag{2}
\]

We now use a finite modular calculation. Set
\[
p=195318521017
\]
and work modulo \(p\). Primality of \(p\) is not needed; all that will matter at the end is that \(p\geq2\). Direct exact iteration of the defining recurrence from \((1,1)\) through index \(3774\) gives
\[
a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p.                         \tag{3}
\]
This is an ordinary finite integer calculation: at each step, for the current exact positive integers \(x,y\), compute \(g=\gcd(x,y)\), replace \((x,y)\) by
\[
\left(y,\;g+\frac{x+y}{g}\right),
\]
and finally reduce the resulting terms modulo \(p\). Some intermediate residue checkpoints, included to make clear the indexing and the calculation leading to (3), are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrr}
n&1&2&3&10&50&100&500&1000&2000&3000&3772&3773&3774\\ \hline
a_n\bmod p&1&1&3&25&711333&6053975&1456413589&168882081718&89924179220&86361476267&21827756562&77940394258&99768150821.
\end{array}
\]
The gcds in this iteration are computed before reduction modulo \(p\); thus this calculation is an exact evaluation of the original nonlinear recurrence, not an attempt to infer gcds from residues.

Introduce shifted terms \(b_n=a_n+1\). Equation (2) implies
\[
b_{3775+k}=b_{3774+k}+b_{3773+k}.                            \tag{4}
\]
Let
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For a column vector, multiplication by \(M\) sends \((u,v)^T\) to \((v,u+v)^T\). Therefore (4), by induction on \(k\), gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773+k}\\b_{3774+k}\end{pmatrix}
\equiv
M^k\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773}\\b_{3774}\end{pmatrix}
pmod p                                                        \tag{5}
\]
for every \(k\geq0\). The case \(k=0\) is immediate. If (5) holds for \(k\), multiplication by \(M\) changes the left-hand pair to
\[
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3774+k}\\b_{3773+k}+b_{3774+k}\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773+(k+1)}\\b_{3774+(k+1)}\end{pmatrix}
\]
by (4), proving the induction step.

We take
\[
K=249580073233.
\]
The necessary matrix power modulo \(p\) is
\[
M^K\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
117378126758&21827756563\\
21827756563&139205883321
\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p.                                                       \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, here is a full repeated-squaring certificate for this finite modular computation. Write
\[
E_j=M^{2^j}\pmod p.
\]
Starting with \(E_0=M\), each following row is obtained simply by squaring the preceding \(2\times2\) matrix and reducing every entry modulo \(p\). Listing a symmetric matrix by the triple \((r,s,t)\) meaning \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}r&s\\s&t\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\), the values are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r}

The binary decomposition used to assemble the desired power is
\[
\begin{aligned}
K={}&1+16+256+4096+8192+32768+65536+2097152\\
 &+67108864+134217728+268435456+8589934592\\
 &+34359738368+68719476736+137438953472.
\end{aligned}                                                  \tag{7}
\]
Equivalently, the nonzero binary positions are
\[
0,4,8,12,13,15,16,21,26,27,28,33,35,36,37.
\]
Multiplying the corresponding matrices \(E_j\) from the table, reducing modulo \(p\), gives precisely the matrix displayed in (6). Thus every part of (6) is reduced to ordinary multiplication and reduction of explicitly displayed integers.

By (3), the initial shifted vector in (5) is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773}\\b_{3774}\end{pmatrix}
\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}77940394259\\99768150822\end{pmatrix}
pmod p.                                                        \tag{8}
\]
Multiplying (6) by (8) gives
\[
M^K\begin{pmatrix}b_{3773}\\b_{3774}\end{pmatrix}
\equiv\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\pmod p.               \tag{9}
\]
Here the two unreduced row sums are, respectively,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&117378126758\cdot77940394259
 +21827756563\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{25mm}=11326212385784681827108
 =57988419771\,p+1,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
&21827756563\cdot77940394259
 +139205883321\cdot99768150822\\
&\hspace{25mm}=15589577514788957011679
 =79816176334\,p+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
These equalities directly verify (9).

Combining (5) and (9) now yields
\[
b_{3773+K}\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad b_{3774+K}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Since \(b_n=a_n+1\), it follows that
\[
a_{3773+K}\equiv0\pmod p,
\qquad a_{3774+K}\equiv0\pmod p.                              \tag{10}
\]
In explicit indices, these are the two consecutive terms
\[
a_{249580077006}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{249580077007}.
\]
Thus, under the assumption (1), both are divisible by \(p\).

Set
\[
X=a_{3774+K},\qquad Y=a_{3773+K},\qquad g=\gcd(X,Y).
\]
Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are positive. By (10), \(p\mid X\) and \(p\mid Y\), so \(p\mid g\). Since \(g>0\) and \(p\geq2\), this implies
\[
g\geq p\geq2.                                                 \tag{11}
\]

Now consider the next index
\[
N=3775+K=249580077008,
\]
which certainly satisfies \(N\geq3775\). The defining recurrence says
\[
a_N=g+\frac{X+Y}{g}.                                          \tag{12}
\]
On the other hand, the assumed formula (1) says
\[
a_N=1+X+Y.                                                     \tag{13}
\]
These two equations cannot both hold when \(X,Y>0\) and \(g\geq2\). Indeed, because \(g\) is the gcd, write
\[
X=gr,\qquad Y=gs
\]
with positive integers \(r,s\). Put \(t=r+s\). Then \(t\geq2\) and \(X+Y=gt\). Equating the right sides of (12) and (13) gives
\[
g+t=1+gt.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
(g-1)(t-1)=0.
\]
But (11) gives \(g-1>0\), while \(t\geq2\) gives \(t-1>0\), a contradiction.

Therefore the first claimed identity cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Consequently it is impossible that, for every such \(n\), all three identities in the conjecture hold. This disproves the stated A355898 conjecture.
